source.title: Erased, but Not Gone: Output Forgetting Is Not True Forgetting
source.authors: T. Yong; W. Ong; C. Chan

record.file_problem: None apparent; full paper text including appendices is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests unlearning and relearning recovery in a new setting: class-level image classification models rather than LLMs. It reports both a small-set relearning attack and linear-probe recovery of forgotten class information.
record.gate_note: The study tests class unlearning, not LLM unlearning. The relearning attack uses five forget samples, and the representation probe trains a new linear classifier on the full dataset. It does not test direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery. The paper also reports CKA, directional alignment, subspace, scaling, and other representation diagnostics; these are summarized in the authors' conclusion but are not listed as separate rows here because the rows focus on the reported attack and direct probe results bearing on the tested claim versions.
record.test_reason: New setting: class unlearning in image classifiers (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10), not LLM knowledge. The study runs its own five-forget-sample relearning attack against unlearned models and compares recovery speed with retrained models (bears on B). It also trains linear probes on frozen backbones to test whether forget-class identity stays linearly accessible (bears on C's blocks-access-not-deletion clause). Output-level forgetting and retain accuracy bear on the output part of A. Treating image classifiers as the 'same kind of system' as the LLMs in the original sources is a judgment call; researchers may weight these results lower.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Precisely: output-level evaluation overestimates class unlearning in image models, and representations stay retraining-inconsistent in a structured way. The faster-than-retrain relearning recovery is shown for SSD and POUR-D. SCRUB recovers only with 0% retain accuracy, and Amnesiac does not recover within budget. The authors scope conclusions to class-level image unlearning and state that LLM validation is absent.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates class-level unlearning in image classifiers using CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet; it does not use the LLM unlearning methods or knowledge and prompt attacks named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by unlearning method: SSD and POUR-D recover earlier than retrains, SCRUB recovers with 0% retain test accuracy, and Amnesiac does not reach the threshold in the evaluated runs. Representation probe outcomes also vary by method.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearned models' penultimate representations fall outside the 10-retrain CKA and cosine-shift reference intervals on all six diagnostics. The exception is POUR-P, inconclusive on two retain diagnostics. Residual mismatch concentrates along the retraining shift direction (Tables 2–3, Fig. 3, 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-level unlearning leaves representation geometry inconsistent with retraining, beyond retraining variability.

record.problems: The empirical setting is class-level image unlearning rather than LLM knowledge unlearning. Relearning tests use five samples and report only a small number of runs for methods (3/3, 2/3, or 0/3); the retrain recovery result is 7/10 models. The paper itself limits validation to class-level image classification and states that LLM validation is absent.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Representation CKA, directional-alignment, and subspace results are discussed in the paper but not separately tabulated here; the selected rows capture the direct relearning attack and linear-probe results relevant to the tested versions.

untested.parts: LLM knowledge unlearning. General ability beyond retain-set accuracy. Attacks other than five-sample relearning and linear probing.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data. Relearning outside CIFAR-10/ResNet-18. LLMs.
Entire version: no prompting, rephrasing or in-context attacks.
Entire version. POUR-P/D are representation-aware methods, but the study does not evaluate any robustness claim for them.

missing.what: Output-level forget and retain accuracy in the scaling settings, e.g. SCRUB forget 67.77% on CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 and 26.50% on TinyImageNet; SSD retain 22.91% on TinyImageNet
t-SNE showing intact forget-class clusters for Amnesiac, SSD and POUR-P/D; SCRUB diffuse (qualitative)
Retain-set probe accuracies (e.g. UNSIR 23.91%, Boundary Shrink 85.19%) needed to read the forget-probe rows

record.verdict_notes: All reader version ids (V1–V3) were invalid and are remapped to A–C. The relearning attack is only on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, and its epoch budget is not stated. Retrained models also reach 90% from five samples, so B evidence rests on recovery speed, not recovery per se. POUR-D, a representation-aware method, recovers fastest, which is weakly relevant to F, but no robustness claim is tested.

versions.untested_parts: LLM-specific methods and general ability beyond the reported retain-set measures are not tested.
Relearning uses five samples from the forgotten class; unrelated or loosely related examples and LLM knowledge are not tested.
No activation-direction ablation is performed. The study probes linear recoverability in image-model representations, not LLM representations.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery are not tested.
No newer counter-method is evaluated for resistance to the listed attacks.
